A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CERES-maize model was not able to express all of the observed data, that the model was able to reproduce data from many lines, but that the model could not distinguish among multiple parameter sets, and that parameters were highly unstable.
the genetic control of anthesis date in maize is not simple, and that the genetic architecture of GSP’s may not resemble that of other quantitative traits.

the CERES-maize model can predict anthesis date for 4,918 lines (91.5% of the data) with an R2 of 0.94, but that the model’s ability to express the phenotypic variation of the remaining 348 lines (6.7%) is highly dependent on the set of site-years used to estimate the parameters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of crop models to predict the phenotypic effects of genotypes in new environments is not straightforward and requires careful attention.

the genetic architecture of phenotypic variation in crop models is likely to be more complex than that of conventional traits, and that model parameters are likely to behave differently from more conventional traits.

, although ecophysiological models can be used to estimate parameters that are correlated with phenotypic traits of interest, these parameters are not necessarily the best means to identify the underlying genetic basis for the traits.
